  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS3" title="In Appendix B Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.3 </span>Propensity estimation via maximum likelihood</span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#A2.SS4" title="In Appendix B Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">B.4 </span>Capabilities as a Special Case of the Propensities Model</span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_appendix"><a href="#A3" title="In Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">C </span>Annotated-demand-levels (ADeLe)</span></a></li>

<br class="ltx_break">Measuring Propensities in AI</h1>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">AI evaluation has primarily focused on measuring capabilities, with formal approaches inspired from Item Response Theory (IRT) being increasingly applied. Yet propensities—the tendencies of models to exhibit particular behaviours—play a central role in determining both performance and safety outcomes.
However, traditional IRT describes a model’s success on a task as a monotonic function of model capabilities and task demands, an approach unsuited to propensities, where both excess and deficiency can be problematic.
Here, we introduce the first formal framework for measuring AI propensities by using a bilogistic formulation for model success, which attributes high success probability when the model’s propensity is within an “ideal band”.
Further, we estimate the limits of the ideal band using LLMs equipped with newly developed task-agnostic rubrics.
Applying our framework to six families of LLM models whose propensities are incited in either direction, we find that we can measure how much the propensity is shifted and what effect this has on the tasks.
Critically, propensities estimated using one benchmark successfully predict behaviour on held-out tasks.
Moreover, we obtain stronger predictive power when combining propensities and capabilities than either separately. More broadly, our framework showcases how rigorous propensity measurements can be conducted and how it yields gains over solely using capability evaluations to predict AI behaviour.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, Propensities, Predictable AI
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18182v1/Figures/fig1.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/294;" width="452" height="294" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An item response curve with propensity <math id="S1.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> representing risk aversion, for a simple financial item: “Would you prefer $10 with 100% probability, $30 with 50% probability, or $500 with 1% probability?”. Extremely low risk-aversion (being reckless) or slight high risk-aversion (being paralysed) are both bad to succeed, setting the two ‘limits’ (<math id="S1.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-3</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S1.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>) of the ‘bilogistic interval’ as the points where the probability of success is around 0.5, with an ideal band in between reaching probability 1 in the middle. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The evaluation of modern AI systems has predominantly focused on measuring capabilities <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Burden et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. While many evaluation approaches simply assess performance on task-specific benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, there is an increasing recognition that, in order to evaluate general-purpose AI systems and extrapolate to new tasks and distributions, it is necessary to determine latent variables of the AI system, such as its capabilities, going beyond task-oriented evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hernández-Orallo, 2017</a>)</cite>. Some approaches derive these “constructs” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cronbach and Meehl, 1955</a>)</cite> from populations of AI systems and benchmarks, such as factor analysis <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Burnell et al., 2023a</a>)</cite> or item response theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Embretson and Reise, 2000</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martínez-Plumed et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, where item (example or benchmark) difficulty and subject (human or AI system) ability are estimated concurrently. However, in order to explain and predict performance in a way that does not depend on the pool of benchmarks or other AI systems, new non-populational methods have emerged based on rubrics that annotate the tasks, making it possible to estimate a wide range of capabilities on commensurate scales for any system and item independently of the rest and thus achieving high predictive and explanatory power <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">OECD, 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, capabilities are not the only constructs that predict and explain behaviour. <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Propensities</span>—systematic tendencies in model behaviour, such as biases, stylistic preferences, personality-like traits, or value alignment—also play a major role.
Beyond the idea of ‘dangerous capabilities’ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shevlane et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, it is now recognised that a sufficient level of capabilities and certain propensities, together, are risk catalysers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ganguli et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gehman et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. For example, consider an AI system with strong capabilities in assigning staff to tasks to maximise productivity. If the system exhibits biases (for certain gender or age) in how it assigns responsibilities, these tendencies can lead to consistently unfair or suboptimal allocations, despite the system being capable of producing optimal solutions when those factors are not present. Similarly, if an AI system has high communication skills, but low tendency for manipulation, then it is less likely that the AI system will succeed in persuasion tasks. In such cases, failure arises from behavioural propensities that distort decision-making instead of insufficient capability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing work on propensities mostly focused on determining bias levels against protected attributes such as gender, race, etc., or tendencies that could lead to harmful or undesirable outputs.
While capability evaluation is increasingly moving from benchmark-sensitive performance scores to distribution-invariant capability constructs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">OECD, 2025</a>)</cite>, the same transition has not yet happened for propensities, with used indicators mostly being mere aggregates of a bias or tendency
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ziegler et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Serapio-García et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. The fundamental reason is the lack of a proper formal model that accounts for propensities in a simple and elegant way similarly to how abilities and difficulty (demands) are contrasted in standard capability models. This is what this paper aims to address.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Specifically, we develop a mathematical model for the evaluation of propensities (Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) by extending the sigmoidal models of Item Response Theory (IRT, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Embretson and Reise, 2000</a></cite>).
We show that our mathematical model recovers a popular IRT capability model as special case, ensuring a unified framework for the measurement of both. Further, we employ LLM annotation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for propensity demands, inspired by measurement scales theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Stevens, 1946</a>)</cite>. We create new benchmarks for four propensity dimensions (red-vs-blue preference, risk aversion, introversion and ultracrepidarianism) and empirically demonstrate that, between systems with similar capability profiles, differences in propensities lead to meaningful and predictable differences in task performance. We also show that capabilities are not enough for predicting performance, with results improving when including propensities. These results suggest that incorporating propensities alongside capabilities is essential for predicting success in a diversity of tasks that rely on both kinds of constructs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Previous work and problem statement</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Capabilities</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In construct-based evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cronbach and Meehl, 1955</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Messick, 1995</a>)</cite>, a capability is a latent, monotonic property of a system that explains and predicts success across tasks. This contrasts with accuracy scores tied to a particular benchmark mix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Srivastava and others, 2022</a>)</cite>, which often have limited explanatory power (which ability has been displayed) and limited predictive power (how performance transfers to novel instances) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bowman and Dahl, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Burnell et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Construct-based evaluation instead separates properties of the <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">subject</em> (the AI system) from properties of the <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">items</em> (task instances): performance becomes predictable from the interaction between a system’s capability level and the difficulty (the demands) posed by an instance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Psychometrics operationalises this via Item Response Theory (IRT), with success probability as a monotonic function of subject ability and item difficulty, both inferred using a population of test takers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rasch, 1960</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Birnbaum, 1968</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lord, 1980</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Embretson and Reise, 2000</a>)</cite>. IRT has also been used in AI <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Martínez-Plumed et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
However, AI enabled two major changes, which reduce the need of populational approaches underlying IRT: (1) the ability of LLMs to cheaply interpret rubrics defining difficulty scales have unlocked the possibility to extract item difficulties from the item only by LLM annotation, and (2) AI systems can be evaluated with thousands of examples, which is usually infeasible for humans. Relying on these opportunities, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2025)</a></cite> (i) defined a set of general capability dimensions together with explicit rubrics that map each instance to an absolute demand level on each dimension; and (ii) estimated LLM capabilities by analysing success rates as a function of these demand levels (i.e., characteristic curves). The resulting per-dimension capability profile supports instance-level explanation (which demands drove success or failure) and, when combined with demand annotations for new tasks, enables anticipating performance beyond the original benchmark. See Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Annotated-demand-levels (ADeLe) ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for further details. We build on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2025)</a></cite> by performing LLM annotation of propensity demand <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">intervals</span> using rubrics.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Propensities</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use propensities to denote systematic tendencies of a model to produce particular kinds of behaviour <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grey and Segerie, 2025</a>)</cite> (e.g., stereotyping, toxicity, sycophancy, extraversion or norm-violating choices). Unlike capabilities, which exhibit a monotonic relationship with performance where higher levels consistently improve outcomes, propensities demonstrate a non-monotonic relationship where both excessive and insufficient levels can be detrimental to performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mischel, 1968</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mischel and Shoda, 1995</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fleeson, 2001</a>)</cite>.
Also, many propensities are better detected through scenario-based instruments such as situational judgment tests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lievens et al., 2008</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In current AI practice, propensities are typically evaluated with collections of prompts or benchmark instances designed to elicit a target tendency, reporting aggregate rates preference gaps, such as for social bias in language modelling and QA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nadeem et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nangia et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parrish et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smith et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, toxic generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gehman et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, or reward–ethics trade-offs and value judgments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hendrycks et al., 2021a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan and others, 2023</a>)</cite>, as well as behavioural tendencies such as sycophancy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sharma et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. While informative as monitoring indicators, these evaluations often (i) collapse behaviour into a single summary statistic (e.g., propensity score) that is sensitive to the benchmark’s mixture/variety of situations; (ii) have a weak situational grounding as they are frequently elicited outside real/consequential scenarios (e.g., ‘‘what would you do’’-style questions in personality trait tests); (iii) conflate propensity with capability (or with refusal/policy mechanisms) when situations vary in difficulty; (iv) lack calibrated demand scales and annotation rubrics that generalise to arbitrary tasks, including tasks where the propensity is irrelevant<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Critically, “neutral demand” (success requires a narrow band, e.g., unbiased decisions) is not the same as “no demand” (the task outcome is unaffected by the propensity).</span></span></span>; (v) lack a formal model of propensity constructs where there is an ideal band for solving a task.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The way forward is similar to what has been achieved with capabilities: building probabilistic models that consider propensities as latent factors to be estimated. However, many propensities are inherently non-monotonic: too little or too much of a tendency can both harm success.
In this work, we operationalise this by introducing a hill-shaped function where the probability that a test taker succeeds on a task is high if its propensity is within a specific demand interval; this incorporates notions from traditional psychometrics—ideal-point (unfolding) models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andrich, 1988</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Roberts et al., 2000</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Conceptualisation</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a task item (or <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">instance</span>) <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, we denote <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> as the binary indicator of whether the considered test taker (in our case, an AI system) succeeded (<math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{1}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{1}=1</annotation></semantics></math>) or failed (<math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{1}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{1}=0</annotation></semantics></math>). In this section, we introduce probabilistic models of the probability of <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}=1</annotation></semantics></math> based on the test taker’s capabilities or propensities and item features.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Capabilities: the 2PL Model</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Item Response Theory (IRT, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Embretson and Reise, 2000</a></cite>), the probability of success is often modelled as a function of the test taker’s <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">capability</em> <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> (a latent value to be inferred) and the item’s difficulty <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and discrimination <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(y_{i}=1\mid\theta,b_{i},a_{i})=\sigma\bigl(a_{i}(\theta-b_{i})\bigr)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y_{i}=1\mid\theta,b_{i},a_{i})=\sigma\bigl(a_{i}(\theta-b_{i})\bigr).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma(x)=(1+e^{-x})^{-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma(x)=(1+e^{-x})^{-1}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the logistic function.
This response curve, referred to as the “two-parameter logistic (2PL)” model, is monotonic with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> (respectively, increasing and decreasing); additionally, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes how sharp the transition from the high-probability to low-probability region is, with the function converging to a step function as <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}\to+\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}\to+\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. Full details (likelihood, estimation and theoretical results) are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Capabilities: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Similarly to what is traditionally done for capabilities (Sec. <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Capabilities: the 2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), we model a <em id="S3.SS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">propensity</em> as a latent, real-valued location parameter <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> on a propensity dimension (e.g., risk aversion, sycophancy, or norm compliance). However, as discussed in Sec. <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Propensities ‣ 2 Previous work and problem statement ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>, in contrast to capability, success on many propensity-relevant instances requires the model to exhibit <em id="S3.SS2.p1.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">neither too little nor too much</em> of the propensity.
We therefore characterise each item <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> by a <em id="S3.SS2.p1.2.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">propensity demand interval</em> <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[b_{l,i},b_{u,i}],withb_{u,i}\geq b_{l,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>≥</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[b_{l,i},b_{u,i}],withb_{u,i}\geq b_{l,i}</annotation></semantics></math>, which specifies the range of propensity levels that yield high probability of success for that item.
To operationalise this, we introduce a bi-logistic model defined as the product of two logistic functions:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E2X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle P\bigl(y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle P\bigl(y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=1\mid\theta,b_{l,i},b_{u,i},a_{l,i},a_{u,i}\bigr)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=1\mid\theta,b_{l,i},b_{u,i},a_{l,i},a_{u,i}\bigr)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.E2Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>=</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E2Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle A_{i}\sigma\bigl(a_{l,i}(\theta-b_{l,i})\bigr)\sigma\bigl(a_{u,i}(b_{u,i}-\theta)\bigr)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle A_{i}\sigma\bigl(a_{l,i}(\theta-b_{l,i})\bigr)\sigma\bigl(a_{u,i}(b_{u,i}-\theta)\bigr),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{l,i},a_{u,i}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{l,i},a_{u,i}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> are two discrimination parameters and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is a normalisation factor. Overall, the function has 2x2 parameters, so we term it “2x2PL”, in line with the psychometric nomenclature. This formulation generalises Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Capabilities: the 2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), to which it converges when <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{l}\to-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{l}\to-\infty</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{u}\to+\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{u}\to+\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, as we show in Sec. <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Capability model as a special case ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>. In what follows, for simplicity, we use a shared slope <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{l,i}=a_{u,i}=a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{l,i}=a_{u,i}=a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, but the results can be generalised to different slopes.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.18182v1/Figures/twosided-2to4ok.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/260;" width="381" height="260" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><img src="2602.18182v1/AC_2DSurfaceExample.png" id="S3.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:405/350;" width="405" height="350" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(Top) Two-sided 2x2PL item response curves for a demand window <math id="S3.F2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-2,4]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-2,4]</annotation></semantics></math> (vertical markers indicate <math id="S3.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.F2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) and <math id="S3.F2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a=1</annotation></semantics></math>. We see the unnormalised function (solid blue) does not reach 1 at the midpoint of the interval, with the naive normalisation (dashed orange) not crossing at 0.5 at the interval limits. Only the final normalisation (dotted green) approximately meets these two requirements. (Bottom) Induced 2D plot showing the agent characteristic surface (Cartesian space of <math id="S3.F2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{l},b_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{l},b_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) for a subject with actual propensity <math id="S3.F2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=-1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1.5</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=-1.5</annotation></semantics></math>, shown as a b line where the centre of the interval is <math id="S3.F2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-1.5</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.F2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N=1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N=1000</annotation></semantics></math> examples. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Normalisation</span>
As a function of <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>, Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) exhibits a hill-shaped curve that smoothly decreases to 0 as <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\to\pm\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>±</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\to\pm\infty</annotation></semantics></math> and achieves high values within the interval <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[b_{l,i},b_{u,i}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[b_{l,i},b_{u,i}]</annotation></semantics></math>. The maximum value occurs at the interval’s midpoint <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{i}=(b_{l,i}+b_{u,i})/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{i}=(b_{l,i}+b_{u,i})/2</annotation></semantics></math>. However, when <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}=1</annotation></semantics></math>, the maximum depends on the interval radius <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i}=(b_{u,i}-b_{l,i})/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i}=(b_{u,i}-b_{l,i})/2</annotation></semantics></math> and remains strictly less than 1. Even when the test taker’s propensity exactly equals <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, the success probability is below 1 and inversely related to the interval width (see the solid blue line in the top panel of Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, where <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}=1</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This behaviour contrasts our intended interpretation of propensity demand intervals. A wider interval should indicate that a broader range of propensity values enables task success, but this should <span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">not</span> imply that narrower intervals necessarily yield lower maximum success probabilities. Consider a concrete example: an AI system exhibits preference bias toward red versus blue objects, and must choose the pot containing more money. In Item 1, the system faces a red pot with $100 and a blue pot with $101. In Item 2, the red pot contains $100 and the blue pot $200. Item 1 requires a narrower propensity range for success—specifically, even a slight preference for red leads to failure, whereas Item 2 tolerates much stronger red preference before failure occurs (as the marginal reward of choosing the blue pot is larger). Crucially, however, the maximum probability of success (achieved, for instance, when the system prefers blue) equals 1 in both cases, regardless of interval width.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">At the same time, the 2PL model for capabilities (Eq. <a href="#S3.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ 3.1 Capabilities: the 2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) assumes value 0.5 when <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, which attributes that specific meaning to <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> on the capability scale for item <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>. As Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) generalises the 2PL model for capabilities, we would ideally maintain that same interpretation for <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{l,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{l,i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{u,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{u,i}</annotation></semantics></math>. However, with <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> fixed independently of <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{l,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{l,i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{u,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{u,i}</annotation></semantics></math>, the value of the function in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) is not, for narrow intervals, close to 0.5.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To address these two concerns,
we first adjust the discrimination parameter to increase with narrower intervals while, at the same time, recover the original <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> when the interval width increases:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\prime}_{i}=a_{i}+e^{1/r_{i}}-1." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\prime}_{i}=a_{i}+e^{1/r_{i}}-1.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">Second, we fix the normalisation factor so that Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) achieves a maximum value of 1 at the midpoint <math id="S3.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=m_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=m_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i}=\bigl[\sigma(a^{\prime}_{i}r_{i})\bigr]^{-2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i}=\bigl[\sigma(a^{\prime}_{i}r_{i})\bigr]^{-2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.2" class="ltx_p">With these adjustments, our final normalised two-sided 2x2PL model becomes:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">This normalisation achieves two key properties: (1) <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(y_{i}=1|\theta=m_{i},b_{l,i},b_{u,i},a_{i})=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y_{i}=1|\theta=m_{i},b_{l,i},b_{u,i},a_{i})=1</annotation></semantics></math> for all interval widths, ensuring that the maximum success probability is independent of how wide the acceptable propensity range is; and (2) <math id="S3.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(y_{i}=1|\theta=b_{l,i},b_{l,i},b_{u,i},a_{i})\approx P(y_{i}=1|\theta=b_{u,i},b_{l,i},b_{u,i},a_{i})\approx 0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y_{i}=1|\theta=b_{l,i},b_{l,i},b_{u,i},a_{i})\approx P(y_{i}=1|\theta=b_{u,i},b_{l,i},b_{u,i},a_{i})\approx 0.5</annotation></semantics></math> for a broad range of parameter values, preserving the boundary interpretation from the 2PL model (Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Boundary behaviour of the Normalized Two-Sided 2x2PL Model ‣ Appendix B Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>). The top panel of Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> illustrates these properties with the normalised curve (dotted green line) compared to alternative normalisations. Other visualisations are available in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS1" title="B.1 Additional visualisations ‣ Appendix B Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Propensity estimation</span>
Given <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1..N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.0835em">.</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.0835em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1..N</annotation></semantics></math> items with corresponding demand windows <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(b_{l,i},b_{u,i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b_{l,i},b_{u,i})</annotation></semantics></math> and observed outcomes <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>, we can estimate the subject’s propensity by maximum likelihood estimation. Writing <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i}(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i}(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> for Eq. (<a href="#S3.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) (with the item-specific <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{l,i},b_{u,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{l,i},b_{u,i}</annotation></semantics></math> and induced <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{i},a^{\prime}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{i},a^{\prime}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>), the log-likelihood is</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Bigl[y_{i}\log p_{i}(\theta)+(1-y_{i})\log\bigl(1-p_{i}(\theta)\bigr)\Bigr]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Bigl[y_{i}\log p_{i}(\theta)+(1-y_{i})\log\bigl(1-p_{i}(\theta)\bigr)\Bigr]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.p8.2" class="ltx_p">and we take <math id="S3.SS2.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{*}=\arg\max_{\theta}\;\ell(\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{*}=\arg\max_{\theta}\;\ell(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> which we solve with standard gradient-based optimisation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Capability model as a special case</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our windowed (propensity) model subsumes the standard monotonic 2PL capability model when “too much” propensity is never detrimental, i.e., when the upper bound is inactive. Starting from Eq. <a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, taking the limit <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{u}\to+\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{u}\to+\infty</annotation></semantics></math> yields <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma(a_{u}(b_{u}-\theta))\to 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma(a_{u}(b_{u}-\theta))\to 1</annotation></semantics></math> for any finite <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a_{u},\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a_{u},\theta)</annotation></semantics></math>, and therefore</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(y=1\mid\theta,b_{l},b_{u},a_{l},a_{u})\;\to\;\sigma(a_{l}(\theta-b_{l}))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em" stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y=1\mid\theta,b_{l},b_{u},a_{l},a_{u})\;\to\;\sigma(a_{l}(\theta-b_{l}))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">which is exactly the standard monotonic 2PL model with <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b=b_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b=b_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a=a_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a=a_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. The same reduction holds for the normalised form (Eq. <a href="#S3.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) as <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{u}\to+\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{u}\to+\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, and for <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{l}\to-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{l}\to-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. See Appendix. <a href="#A2.SS4" title="B.4 Capabilities as a Special Case of the Propensities Model ‣ Appendix B Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.4</span></a> for rigorous proofs.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Methods and experimental setting</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Propensities and rubrics</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To test our methodology, we first devise hand-crafted rubrics to automate propensity annotation with LLMs. Each rubric consists of a general definition of the propensity and a detailed explanation for levels -3 (or below), -2, -1, 0, +1, +2 and +3 (or above). Each level of the rubric also includes some examples of annotations (anchors) so that the annotator has a better understanding of the differences between levels and intervals. We test four propensity demands:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S4.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Red vs Blue Colour Bias</span>: how strongly a task invites or permits
preferences for red (positive) over blue (negative) to influence the answer or the action of the agent, relative to task-relevant factors.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Risk Aversion/Seeking</span>: how strongly a task invites or permits preferences about not taking a risk (positive) versus taking a risk (negative) to influence an answer, relative to expected value considerations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Extraversion/Introversion</span>: how strongly a task invites or permits a preference for social engagement (positive) versus internal isolation (negative), relative to instrumental behaviour required to maximise the stated utility function in social situations.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ultracrepidarianism/Prudence</span>: how strongly a task invites or permits a preference for either pronouncement or answering about things the agent does not know or is unsure of (positive), or keeping a prudent and reserved position of not acting or answering (negative), relative to instrumental behaviour required for the task.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Following the methodology of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2025)</a></cite>, we use a language model to automate the process of annotation. We employed GPT-4.1 as the annotator model, which is a compromise of quality of annotations and cost of annotation per instance (to be able to scale to benchmarks with thousands of examples and on-the-fly annotation). The rubrics for each propensity can be found in the supplementary material (external to this paper). The complete annotation prompts used for GPT-4.1 are available in Appendix  <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Annotation prompts ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Propensity datasets</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although our methodology theoretically allows us to infer the propensity parameter from arbitrary datasets, the performance on typical datasets is often dominated by factors other than propensity bias. This gives a relatively low signal-to-noise ratio for fitting the propensity parameter. To counteract this, we design low-difficulty datasets where task success is not bottlenecked by capabilities, ensuring that responses more directly reflect propensity biases.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each propensity, we design a multiple-choice question dataset with three options. Two of these options reflect the natural choices of agents biased toward each pole of the propensity spectrum. The third choice is designed to never be selected by strongly biased agents, either because it is unrelated to the propensity or because it is clearly inferior regardless of which bias the agent holds. This third option lowers the performance of random agents while also enabling a larger variety of item propensity demand intervals. We show examples in Table <a href="#A4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix D Propensity datasets ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. Each dataset contains approximately 250 samples; exact counts are provided in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Propensity datasets ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>, which also includes representative examples for each propensity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Note that while we infer the propensity of a model from synthetic datasets, the inferred propensity can still be used on out-of-distribution samples to predict performance, by automatically annotating these new samples on the fly.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Inference of biased models</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use six families of large language models, including two proprietary systems (GPT-4o, o1) and ten open-weight models, ranging from 3B to 70B parameters, and including both standard instruction-tuned variants and reasoning-specialized models. We provide the details of the models used in <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.3 Inference of biased models ‣ 4 Methods and experimental setting ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">LLMs used for inference, along with details about parameters (Params), whether they are distilled (Dist.) and whether they are reasoning models (Reas.) along with the name that we use through the paper to refer to the models.</span></figcaption>
<div id="S4.T1.5" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:92.6pt;vertical-align:-44.6pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-75.7pt,20.3pt) scale(0.695120446260912,0.695120446260912) ;">
<table id="S4.T1.5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T1.5.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S4.T1.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S4.T1.5.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Params</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S4.T1.5.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dist.</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;"><span id="S4.T1.5.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reas.</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T1.5.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">Llama-3.3-70B-Inst (Llama 3.3) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori and others, 2024</a>)</cite></td>
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">70B</td>
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">✗</td>
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">✗</td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T1.5.1.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding-left:2.5pt;padding-right:2.5pt;">Llama-3.2-3B-Inst (Llama 3.2) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grattafiori and others, 2024</a>)</cite></td>
