</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For each LLM and propensity dataset, we applied seven graded system prompts, from extremely biased (+3/-3) through mildly biased (+1/-1) to unbiased (0), as well as using the LLM without any system prompt. This unprompted configuration should represent the default propensity behaviour of the LLM. Table <a href="#A6.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix F Biasing system prompts for risk aversion ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> in
Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Biasing system prompts for risk aversion ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a> details the prompt structure using the risk-seeking dimension as an illustrative example; the complete set of prompts for all benchmarks is provided in the supplementary material.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For each combination of propensity dataset, model, and biasing system prompt, we collect the binary outcomes <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> indicating whether the model selected the correct
option for each item <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>. To ensure consistent evaluation across all LLMs and samples, we apply an LLM-as-a-judge procedure using GPT-4.1 to extract the intended selection from model outputs by checking semantic equivalence to the valid answer option.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These outcomes, together with the annotated item-level propensity demand intervals, allow us to estimate the LLM’s propensity under each prompt condition via Equation <a href="#S3.E6" title="Equation 6 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Predicting Outcome</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We investigate whether propensity levels provide additional predictive power beyond capability demands when estimating LLM performance. To this end, we train assessors (a classifier predicting whether the base LLM is going to be correct or incorrect <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hernández-Orallo et al., 2022</a>)</cite>) that rely solely on item-level capability demands and compare them against assessors that additionally incorporate propensities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments focus on a compiled benchmark of 360 question–context pairs, evenly split between answerable (180) and unanswerable (180) items, sampled from the TimeQA and MentalQA datasets, where ultracrepidarianism should play an important role, along with capabilities (e.g., metacognition). In each instance, a question and its supporting context are provided, and the agent is required to answer the question if it can be inferred from the context; otherwise, the agent should indicate that the question is unanswerable. Note that this is not the benchmark about ultracrepidarianism explained in Sec. <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Propensity datasets ‣ 4 Methods and experimental setting ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> that we used to infer the LLM’s propensity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For each item, we annotate 18 capability dimensions following the ADeLe framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. In addition, we also annotate the propensity levels of all instances along four dimensions: Ultracrepidarianism, Extraversion/Introversion, Blue/Red, and Risk aversion/seeking, using the methodology described in the previous section. We get a 22-dimensional vector per instance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate 10 LLMs, each instantiated at three Ultracrepidarianism levels (-2, 0, +2), yielding a total of 30 model configurations. LLMs with a propensity level of -2 tend toward diffidence, potentially withholding correct answers, whereas models with a propensity level of +2 exhibit overextension, producing confident but often incorrect responses beyond their knowledge boundaries.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To assess the contribution of propensity information, we train a Random Forest assessor using three feature sets: (1) 18 capability dimensions only; (2) 18 capability dimensions plus one Ultracrepidarianism propensity; and (3) 18 capability dimensions combined with all 4 propensity dimensions.</p>
</div>

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S4.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Measured propensity level across incitation levels from -3 to +3 and unprompted for Qwen 3-4B-I in the Introversion dataset. This figure and all the combinations for other LLMs and datasets are included in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Propensity plots ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Assessors are trained to predict instance-level model performance for these three configurations. We employ 10-fold instance-wise cross-validation, using a minimum of 50 samples per split to control tree growth and reduce overfitting. Performance is evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), which serves as our primary metric for comparing the assessors’ predictive power across feature configurations in a way that can compare LLMs with low and high performances.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first focus on the MLE inference and illustrate the agent characteristic curves for propensities.
Next, we explore how much LLMs can be biased for the four propensities (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Inference of biased models ‣ 4 Methods and experimental setting ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>) as recovered with our MLE estimation. Finally, we analyse how much the propensities can add in predicting performance compared to using capabilities only (Sec. <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Predicting Outcome ‣ 4 Methods and experimental setting ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Predicting Outcome ‣ 4 Methods and experimental setting ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the empirical propensity surfaces for different incitation levels of Qwen 3-4B-I in the Introversion dataset. As the incitation level moves from -3 to +3, the measured propensity (black line) moves accordingly from bottom left to top right. The unprompted model’s measured propensity is -0.13, showing that Qwen-4B-I, when not incited to display any specific behaviour, displays a very tiny preference towards introversion.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Predicting Outcome ‣ 4 Methods and experimental setting ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, there are substantial differences for Red vs Blue Colour Bias among models when they are not incited: models like DS-R1-Qwen32B and Qwen-3-4B exhibit propensity levels very close to 0 (an expected indifference towards red or blue), while models like Llama3.2 and Gemma3 display mild biases towards red.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Regarding Ultracrepidarianism, most unprompted models tend to display a low level of caution when not knowing the answer (negative small propensities levels). When inciting models to display ultracrepidarian tendencies, one thing to remark is the propensity levels of Llama 3.2. (all negative), showing either failure to follow the system prompts (due to insufficient capabilities) or resistance to follow them. This result suggests that our procedure allows testing the robustness of models against incitation attempts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Predicting Outcome ‣ 4 Methods and experimental setting ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows different patterns for Risk Aversion and Extraversion/Introversion: Llama 3.2 displays extreme risk-seeking when not incited, while unprompted Deepseek models tend to be more risk-averse. Unprompted models display moderately neutral Introversion/Extraversion propensity levels.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Now we focus on the incremental predictive power propensities provide to assessors. Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.4 Predicting Outcome ‣ 4 Methods and experimental setting ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows that for most models, assessors trained on capability demands only are outperformed by assessors trained on capability demands and Ultracrepidarianism demands or capability demands and all propensity demands, usually by <math id="S5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.02" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.02</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.02</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S5.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+0.03" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>0.03</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+0.03</annotation></semantics></math> AUCROC points (with the exception of Qwen 3-4B-I). This pattern is observed independent of the incitation level as well, showing these findings generalise across models and incitation levels.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduced a new mathematical model to represent propensities that is intuitive—demands are seen as ‘ideal bands’ within which a model’s propensity must be to have high probability of success—and simple in its most basic configuration—bilogistic formulation with two parameters per item (assuming the slopes are set in an equal manner for all items) and one propensity value per subject to be estimated. However, the model allows for item-specific adjustment of the slopes of the interval ends if necessary. In accordance with IRT nomenclature, we termed the model 2x2PL. We revealed important theoretical analysis: our propensity model is a generalisation of the traditional 2PL capability model in psychometrics, facilitating understanding and integration, and our normalisation meets a balance between probability one in the middle point in the interval and probability close to 0.5 at the interval extremes. We designed rubrics to annotate examples with propensity demand intervals and showed that this annotation can be used to estimate propensity in the scale set based on the rubric, allowing for a commensurate comparison of the same and different propensities across datasets. This actually makes it possible to use the annotated propensity dimensions along capabilities to predict performance, showing that propensities contribute additional predictive power. The abstraction of both capabilities and propensities is more robust against overfitting to a particular dataset and shows predictability across datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As the first formal propensities model conceptualising demands as a soft ‘ideal band’, our model has some limitations. We think that model propensities (and not only demands) could also be modelled with two parameters rather than one. For the moment the error of estimation of a given propensity can be used as an indication of how much the propensity can be incited or fixed at a particular level, but this is now also affected by the sample size and other factors. Also, experiments with agents will show a more dominant effect of propensities, especially in long-term scenarios or social situations, where propensities play a larger role, compared to capabilities only, in predicting performance and safety.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This work sits within the broader agenda of deriving a catalogue of capabilities and propensities that are explanatory and predictive of AI performance and safety, represented in standard scales with rubrics that are interpretable and applied automatically. This enables extracting AI system profiles derived from evidence specific to the AI system itself and not affected by other current or future AI systems.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper introduces a new model for evaluating propensities that can serve to integrate different perspectives for evaluating non-capability traits, such as bias, personality, values, etc. Measuring these latent traits accurately is crucial for both safe and ethical applications of machine learning and other AI systems. Through the mathematical model and the predictability angle, we can also frame propensities in a way that is more familiar to machine learning, optimising the modelling and inference of propensities and predictive models from them. Accordingly, we think this paper can foster a wider and more comprehensive discussion between ethical and safety perspectives on system deployment, and the short-term and long-term impacts of artificial intelligence.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Capabilities: additional details</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We model the probabilistic relation between an agent’s ability and item difficulty (the agent characteristic curve) using the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model:</p>
<table id="A1.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.E8"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle P(y=1\mid\theta,b,a)=\sigma\left(a(\theta-b)\right)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-a(\theta-b)\right)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle P(y=1\mid\theta,b,a)=\sigma\left(a(\theta-b)\right)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left(-a(\theta-b)\right)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes success, <math id="A1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> is the agent (or subject) ability parameter, <math id="A1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b\in\mathbb{R}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b\in\mathbb{R}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> is the item difficulty parameter, <math id="A1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a\in\mathbb{R}^{+}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\in\mathbb{R}^{+}</annotation></semantics></math> is the discrimination (steepness), and <math id="A1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is the logistic sigmoid.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For <math id="A1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> items with known <math id="A1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a_{i},b_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a_{i},b_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> and responses <math id="A1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, the log-likelihood for <math id="A1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is:</p>
<table id="A1.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Bigl[y_{i}\log\sigma\!\bigl(a_{i}(\theta-b_{i})\bigr)+(1-y_{i})\log\!\bigl(1-\sigma(a_{i}(\theta-b_{i}))\bigr)\Bigr]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.437em;" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.146em;" width="1.146em"><mi>log</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Bigl[y_{i}\log\sigma\!\bigl(a_{i}(\theta-b_{i})\bigr)+(1-y_{i})\log\!\bigl(1-\sigma(a_{i}(\theta-b_{i}))\bigr)\Bigr]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The maximum likelihood estimate of ability is:</p>
<table id="A1.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{*}=\arg\max_{\theta}\ \ell(\theta)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>θ</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{*}=\arg\max_{\theta}\ \ell(\theta)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Empirically, the item characteristic curve (ICC) for a fixed agent can be estimated as the fraction of successes at each difficulty:</p>
<table id="A1.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E11.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{P}_{\text{emp}}(b)=\frac{\sum_{i:b_{i}=b}y_{i}}{\sum_{i:b_{i}=b}1}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>emp</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mi>y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{P}_{\text{emp}}(b)=\frac{\sum_{i:b_{i}=b}y_{i}}{\sum_{i:b_{i}=b}1}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p2.4" class="ltx_p">The parametric logistic model can then be fit to these empirical proportions to recover agent ability <math id="A1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> and optionally discrimination <math id="A1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>.
This is the standard framework for agent capabilities and item difficulties in 2PL-IRT, using logistic and empirical estimation.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="A1.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{If}\quad\hat{P}_{\text{emp}}(b)\approx\sigma(a(\theta-b))" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>If</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mtext>emp</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{If}\quad\hat{P}_{\text{emp}}(b)\approx\sigma(a(\theta-b))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Then, fitting the logistic curve to the empirical success rate implies</p>
<table id="A1.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\!\bigl(a(\theta^{\mathrm{fit}}-b)\bigr)\;\approx\;\hat{P}_{\mathrm{emp}}(b),\qquad\theta^{\mathrm{fit}}\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\theta^{*}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mpadded style="width:0.437em;" width="0.437em"><mi>σ</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mi>fit</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em" rspace="0.280em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.558em">≈</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>emp</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mi>fit</mi></msup><munderover accent="true" accentunder="true"><mo>→</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">N</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em" stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em" mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><mphantom></mphantom></munderover><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\!\bigl(a(\theta^{\mathrm{fit}}-b)\bigr)\;\approx\;\hat{P}_{\mathrm{emp}}(b),\qquad\theta^{\mathrm{fit}}\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\theta^{*},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the MLE.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem A.1</span></span><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Suppose <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\sigma(a(\theta-b_{i})))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi>Bernoulli</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\sigma(a(\theta-b_{i})))</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1,\ldots,N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1,\ldots,N</annotation></semantics></math>, and let <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{P}_{\mathrm{emp}}(b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>emp</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{P}_{\mathrm{emp}}(b)</annotation></semantics></math> denote the empirical mean success at each difficulty <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> be the maximum likelihood estimate for ability using the logistic model, and <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{fit}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{fit}</annotation></semantics></math> the ability parameter obtained by least-squares fitting a logistic curve to <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{P}_{\mathrm{emp}}(b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>emp</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{P}_{\mathrm{emp}}(b)</annotation></semantics></math> across <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, as <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{b}\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{b}\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math> for each difficulty <math id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta^{fit}\xrightarrow{p}\theta^{*}\xrightarrow{p}\theta," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>θ</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mover accent="true"><mo>→</mo><mo mathsize="0.700em">𝑝</mo></mover><msup><mi>θ</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mover accent="true"><mo>→</mo><mo mathsize="0.700em">𝑝</mo></mover><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta^{fit}\xrightarrow{p}\theta^{*}\xrightarrow{p}\theta,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i.e., both procedures recover the true ability.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text">Apply the law of large numbers to observe that, for each <math id="A1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>,
<math id="A1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{P}_{\mathrm{emp}}(b)\to\sigma(a(\theta-b))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>emp</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{P}_{\mathrm{emp}}(b)\to\sigma(a(\theta-b))</annotation></semantics></math>
almost surely. Fitting a logistic curve to these empirical proportions (by least-squares or maximum likelihood) then yields consistent estimators for the parameters, as does direct maximisation of the likelihood. Thus, both procedures are asymptotically equivalent.
∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recall that a <em id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">propensity</em> is a latent scalar location parameter <math id="A2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>,
while each item specifies an acceptable window of demands <math id="A2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[b_{l},b_{u}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[b_{l},b_{u}]</annotation></semantics></math> (with <math id="A2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{l}&lt;b_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{l}&lt;b_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>).
Unless stated otherwise, we use a shared slope <math id="A2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{l}=a_{u}=a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{l}=a_{u}=a</annotation></semantics></math>. The resulting <em id="A2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">item response curve</em> (IRC) in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) is</p>
<table id="A2.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E14.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="P(y=1\mid\theta,b_{l,i},b_{u},a)=\Bigr[\sigma(a^{\prime}r)\Bigr]^{-2}\cdot\sigma(a^{\prime}(\theta-b_{l}))\cdot\sigma(a^{\prime}(b_{u}-\theta))." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" mathsize="1.600em" rspace="0em">[</mo></mrow><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>σ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y=1\mid\theta,b_{l,i},b_{u},a)=\Bigr[\sigma(a^{\prime}r)\Bigr]^{-2}\cdot\sigma(a^{\prime}(\theta-b_{l}))\cdot\sigma(a^{\prime}(b_{u}-\theta)).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This function is hill-shaped: it is near <math id="A2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> only for propensities well inside the window and decays towards <math id="A2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> as <math id="A2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> moves outside the window.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Additional visualisations</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ B.1 Additional visualisations ‣ Appendix B Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> complements Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> (top) by showing four demand windows of varying widths and, crucially, how different normalisation choices affect both the peak and the boundary calibration. Figure <a href="#A2.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ B.1 Additional visualisations ‣ Appendix B Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> provides a 2D view of the induced <em id="A2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">agent characteristic surface</em> over the <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(b_{l},b_{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b_{l},b_{u})</annotation></semantics></math> space (and the rotated <math id="A2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(m,b_{u}-b_{l})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(m,b_{u}-b_{l})</annotation></semantics></math> coordinates).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F4" class="ltx_figure">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="A2.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Four propensity item response curves using <math id="A2.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{l}=a_{u}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{l}=a_{u}=1</annotation></semantics></math> for the following items, each of them characterised by an interval of demands. Top left: [-5,5], Top right: [-1.5,2.5], Bottom left: [0,1], Bottom right; [0.5,1]. The original function as a product of two logistic functions corresponding to Eq. (<a href="#S3.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) is shown in solid blue. We see that it only approaches 1 for the middle of the interval and 0.5 in the extremes, as desired, for wide intervals. For short intervals, the values fall quite below the desired values of 1 and 0.5.
Finally, the proposed normalisation in dotted red, shown in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), finds a good tradeoff between reaching 1 in the middle, close to 0.5 in the extremes, while respecting the slope for wide intervals. </span></figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F5.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="A2.F5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Agent characteristic surface over window parameters.<span id="A2.F5.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Example surface for a fixed propensity <math id="A2.F5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=-1.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1.5</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=-1.5</annotation></semantics></math> (yellow line) with shared slope <math id="A2.F5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a=1</annotation></semantics></math>, evaluated on randomly-generated windows in <math id="A2.F5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-5,5]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-5,5]</annotation></semantics></math>.
<em id="A2.F5.7.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Left:</em> Cartesian window space <math id="A2.F5.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(b_{l},b_{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(b_{l},b_{u})</annotation></semantics></math>. <em id="A2.F5.7.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Right:</em> rotated coordinates where the horizontal axis is the window centre <math id="A2.F5.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=(b_{u}+b_{l})/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=(b_{u}+b_{l})/2</annotation></semantics></math> and the vertical axis is the window width <math id="A2.F5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b_{u}-b_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b_{u}-b_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. The figure illustrates why naive moment-based summaries can be biased when the observed windows are not symmetrically distributed around <math id="A2.F5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>; this motivates maximum
likelihood estimation (Appendix §<a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Propensity estimation via maximum likelihood ‣ Appendix B Two-sided 2PL propensity model: additional details ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Boundary behaviour of the Normalized Two-Sided 2x2PL Model</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this appendix, we rigorously analyse the behaviour of the normalized propensity response curve (Eq. <a href="#S3.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 3.2 Propensities: the two-sided 2x2PL Model ‣ 3 Conceptualisation ‣ Capabilities Ain’t All You Need:Measuring Propensities in AI" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) at the boundary points <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=b_{l,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=b_{l,i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=b_{u,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=b_{u,i}</annotation></semantics></math>. We demonstrate that the probability of success at these boundaries is approximately <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.5</annotation></semantics></math> across a wide range of parameter values, preserving the interpretability inherited from the standard 2PL model for capabilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For notational convenience, we drop the item subscript <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> throughout this appendix. Recall that the normalized model is:</p>
<table id="A2.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(y=1\mid\theta,b_{l},b_{u},a)=A\cdot\sigma(a^{\prime}(\theta-b_{l}))\cdot\sigma(a^{\prime}(b_{u}-\theta))," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(y=1\mid\theta,b_{l},b_{u},a)=A\cdot\sigma(a^{\prime}(\theta-b_{l}))\cdot\sigma(a^{\prime}(b_{u}-\theta)),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r=(b_{u}-b_{l})/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r=(b_{u}-b_{l})/2</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the half-width of the propensity demand interval, <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\prime}=a+e^{1/r}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\prime}=a+e^{1/r}-1</annotation></semantics></math> is the adjusted discrimination parameter, and <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=[\sigma(a^{\prime}r)]^{-2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=[\sigma(a^{\prime}r)]^{-2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the normalisation factor.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">B.2.1 </span>Probability at the Boundaries</h4>

<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first derive an explicit expression for the probability at the interval boundaries.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="A2.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma B.1</span></span><span id="A2.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">At <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=b_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=b_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="A2.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=b_{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=b_{u}</annotation></semantics></math>, the probability of success equals:</span></p>
<table id="A2.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{\mathrm{boundary}}:=P(y=1\mid\theta\in\{b_{l},b_{u}\},b_{l},b_{u},a)=\frac{1}{2\bigl[\sigma(a^{\prime}r)^{2}+(1-\sigma(a^{\prime}r))^{2}\bigr]}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>boundary</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{\mathrm{boundary}}:=P(y=1\mid\theta\in\{b_{l},b_{u}\},b_{l},b_{u},a)=\frac{1}{2\bigl[\sigma(a^{\prime}r)^{2}+(1-\sigma(a^{\prime}r))^{2}\bigr]}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">By symmetry of the model, it suffices to consider <math id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta=b_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta=b_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. We have:</span></p>
<table id="A2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A2.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sigma(a^{\prime}(\theta-b_{l}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>θ</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sigma(a^{\prime}(\theta-b_{l}))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sigma(0)=\tfrac{1}{2}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sigma(0)=\tfrac{1}{2},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A2.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\sigma(a^{\prime}(b_{u}-\theta))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\sigma(a^{\prime}(b_{u}-\theta))</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\sigma(a^{\prime}(b_{u}-b_{l}))=\sigma(2a^{\prime}r)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\sigma(a^{\prime}(b_{u}-b_{l}))=\sigma(2a^{\prime}r).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.SSS1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text">Therefore:</span></p>

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
